sources.title: INVEST and SMART
sources.citation: Bill Wake, "INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks" (xp123.com, 2003)

claims.statement: The origin of the INVEST acronym and its six definitions; the SMART task companion (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-boxed); the canonical wording "Small" (not "Sized appropriately")

sources.title: The 3 Cs
sources.citation: Ron Jeffries, "Essential XP: Card, Conversation, Confirmation" (ronjeffries.com, 2001)

claims.statement: The origin and definition of the three components; the card's small size as a size signal; Confirmation as the acceptance test

sources.title: The story template
sources.citation: Mike Cohn. "What Is a User Story Template and Why Does It Work So Well?" (Mountain Goat Software)

claims.statement: The three-part "As a / I want / so that" template and the who/what/why rationale; the Connextra format (commonly credited to Rachel Davies, ~2001), popularized but not invented by Cohn (2004)

sources.title: User stories (canonical book)
sources.citation: Mike Cohn, "User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development" (Addison-Wesley, 2004)

claims.statement: The canonical generalization of user stories; the template, the application of INVEST, and the conversation-over-documentation framing

sources.title: Splitting: SPIDR
sources.citation: Mike Cohn, "Five Simple but Powerful Ways to Split User Stories" (Mountain Goat Software)

claims.statement: The SPIDR model (Spike, Path, Interface, Data, Rules) with worked examples; "I" is Interface (singular); Spike as the last-resort, knowledge-only move

sources.title: Splitting: the flowchart
sources.citation: Richard Lawrence / Humanizing Work. "The Humanizing Work Guide to Splitting User Stories"

claims.statement: The splitting-pattern flowchart; the nine patterns (Workflow Steps, Operations/CRUD, Business Rule Variations, Variations in Data, Data Entry Methods, Major Effort, Simple/Complex, Deferred Performance/NFRs, Break Out a Spike); the preconditions; the two evaluation rules

sources.title: Vertical slicing: the walking skeleton
sources.citation: Alistair Cockburn, "Crystal Clear" / "Writing Effective Use Cases" (Walking Skeleton), via the c2 wiki

claims.statement: The walking skeleton as a tiny end-to-end implementation linking the main architectural components; production code with tests; distinct from a prototype or a research spike

sources.title: Backlog refinement
sources.citation: Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland, "The Scrum Guide" (2020)

claims.statement: Product Backlog refinement as the ongoing act of breaking down and further defining items (description / order / size); sizing as the Developers' responsibility; not a prescribed event; items doable within one Sprint are "ready"; the "estimate" (2017) → "size" (2020) wording change
